Graydon Hoare began developing Rust in 2006, and Mozilla Research sponsored the project from 2009 [2]. Its first public release arrived in 2010, and version 1.0 followed in 2015 [2].

Memory safety protects programs from buffer overflows and dangling pointers [3]. C, C++, and Fortran allow arbitrary pointer arithmetic without bounds checking, which leaves them memory-unsafe [3].

Java achieves safety through runtime checks of array bounds and pointer dereferences [3]. Rust takes a different route. Its syntax resembles C++, yet it guarantees memory safety without a garbage collector [2].

Algebraic data types and pattern matching add further structure to Rust code [1]. Together, these features deliver low-level performance alongside guarantees that many systems languages leave to the programmer.","sources":"[1] Wikipedia: Rust (programming language)

Rust also provides structs, enums, traits, and methods as alternatives to traditional object-oriented programming, without relying on classes or inheritance.

Summary: Memory safety is the state of being protected from various software bugs and security vulnerabilities when dealing with memory access, such as buffer overflows and dangling pointers. For example, Java is memory-safe because its runtime error detection checks array bounds and pointer dereferences. By contrast, programming languages like C, C++, and Fortran allow arbitrary pointer arithmetic with pointers implemented as direct memory addresses with no provision for bounds checking, making them memory-unsafe.
